title: Countable vs Uncountable Food Nouns
description: Distinguish between countable items (apples, eggs) and uncountable food/drink (water, rice, bread).
objectives: Categorize everyday food items into countable and uncountable nouns
Use 'a/an' and plural numbers with countable nouns, avoiding them with uncountable nouns
Apply container/measurement counters to uncountable foods (a glass of water, a slice of bread)

sections.title: The Logic of Countable vs. Uncountable
sections.content:
In English, nouns are fundamentally divided into **Countable (C)** and **Uncountable (U)**:

### 1. Countable Nouns
- Things we can count as individual units: *one apple, two apples, three apples*.
- Can be singular or plural.
- Take **a / an** in singular (*an egg, a sandwich*).

### 2. Uncountable Nouns
- Liquids, grains, powders, masses, and concepts: *water, milk, rice, sugar, bread, cheese*.
- Cannot be counted directly (*never 'two rices' or 'three milks'*).
- Have **no plural form** (-s is not added).
- Never take **a / an** directly (*never 'a bread' or 'a water'*).

### Using Partitive Counters
To measure uncountable items, we use a container or measurement counter:
- *a glass of water* / *two bottles of water*
- *a slice of bread* / *two loaves of bread*
- *a cup of tea* / *two cups of tea*
- *a bowl of rice* / *a kilo of sugar*

callouts.title: The 'Bread' False Friend
callouts.text: In Urdu, 'روٹی' is easily counted ('دو روٹیاں'). But in English, **bread** is strictly UNCOUNTABLE! Say: **a slice of bread** or **two pieces of bread**, never *'two breads'*.

callouts.title: Verb Agreement with Uncountable Nouns
callouts.text: Uncountable nouns always take a SINGULAR verb: **Water is essential**, **Rice is delicious**.

sections.title: Lesson Summary
summaryPoints: Countable nouns can be counted individually (an apple, two apples; an egg, three eggs).
Uncountable nouns are masses or liquids (water, milk, bread, rice, sugar, tea).
Uncountable nouns have no plural and take singular verbs (Rice is delicious).
Measure uncountables with counters: a glass of water, a slice of bread, a cup of tea.
Use 'How many' for countables; use 'How much' for uncountables.
